about.title: About
about.headline: I take the half of the frontend that usually breaks
body: I am Viacheslav Androsov, a frontend engineer with four years of production experience. I started with Web3 interfaces on outsourcing, moved through B2B and FinTech products, and now work on the core of a corporate low-code platform: the editor engine, undo across operations, the frame budget.

What interests me is not the mockup but what sits behind it: how the state is arranged, what happens between frames, why a table starts stuttering at five hundred rows and what to do about it. I work in both React and Vue — not "familiar with both", but two production codebases I had to switch between mid-week.

Almost everything I have built is under NDA and cannot be linked. So this site is arranged differently: every claim that carries a number is rebuilt as a demo you can run right here and watch the counter.

principles.title: Measure first, then write
principles.body: Optimising without measuring is guessing. Twice while building these demos the measurement showed that the "slow" version was in fact fast, and the demo had to be rewritten rather than the wording adjusted.

principles.title: Boundaries over polish
principles.body: FSD, public APIs per slice, a linter that catches an import going upwards. Fifty modules and three teams in one repository survive on hard boundaries; they do not survive on agreements.

principles.title: Tests where mistakes are expensive
principles.body: Not for a coverage number. A buffer collapse that quietly changes data is caught only by a property over generated sessions; a panel printing the wrong schema, only by a test tying it to the validator.

undoRedo.title: Undo buffer
undoRedo.lead: Drag the blocks, add one, delete one, rename one. Every gesture writes actions into a single buffer, and the buffer collapses before it is sent.
undoRedo.connecting: Now pick the second block — the link appears, or goes away.
undoRedo.hint: Drag a block, or tap one to select it. A whole drag is one action — ⌘Z undoes the gesture, not a frame of it.
undoRedo.coverage: Six action types here, forty-odd in the editor. The mechanism does not count them.

canvasFps.title: The frame budget
canvasFps.lead: One scene, one animation, two ways of getting a frame onto the screen. Flip the mode and watch the counter: the difference is not the machine, it is what the code finds to do between frames.
canvasFps.canvas: A field of blocks and links
canvasFps.hint: The modes are measured one at a time: there is a single main thread, and two scenes side by side would fight over it. The first thirty frames after a switch are thrown away as warm-up. Hit pause and compare the “loop” line.
canvasFps.naiveNote: Block positions live in reactive state, and the frame repaints the whole scene through left/top — properties that go through layout. Then a pass over the links reads each block's rectangle and immediately places a link from it: measure, write, measure, write. Every write dirties layout, and every next measurement makes the browser recompute it synchronously, in the middle of the frame.
canvasFps.budgetNote: Same work — every block and every link is repositioned, with no cleverness about updating only what changed. Two things differ: coordinates come from the array instead of being read back off the DOM, so nothing forces a layout mid-pass; and only transform is written, which reaches the compositor without going through layout. While paused, no frame is scheduled at all.

txTable.title: A table under live data
txTable.lead: Five hundred transactions, and a mock socket changing statuses every second. The highlight is not decoration: a row lights up at the exact moment React repainted it. Turn virtualisation or memoisation off and watch what lights up.
txTable.hint: The data is synthetic: merchant ids are generated, amounts are random. What is closed is the client's code, not the render strategy.
txTable.note: Virtualisation keeps a couple of dozen rows in the DOM instead of five hundred, so scrolling stops depending on the length of the list. Memoisation solves the other half: a status update repaints one row rather than the grid. It only works because the update leaves untouched rows as the very same objects — memo on top of a fresh copy of the array would not save a single render.

dynamicForm.title: A form that knows its own rules
dynamicForm.lead: Switch the payout method and it is not just the field set that changes — so does the schema the form validates against. It is printed in full on the right: not a picture of the schema, but its source, built from the same rules the validation runs on.
dynamicForm.hint: The schema follows more than the method: for a crypto payout the address is checked against the network you picked — change it and watch the pattern. Values the new schema has no place for are dropped: an IBAN must not travel along with a card payout.
dynamicForm.note: The rules are written once, as a list. Both the Zod object that validates and the text beside it are built from that list. There is nowhere for them to drift apart — and a test holds it: the panel must print every rule the schema validates by.
